name: Chapter 3: Reproductive Health
description: Reproductive health programmes, population and contraception, MTP, sexually transmitted infections, infertility and ART

cards.definition: Total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social

cards.term: When is a society called reproductively healthy?
cards.definition: People have physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects

cards.term: India’s distinction in reproductive health programmes?
cards.definition: Among the first countries to start national action plans for total reproductive health as a social goal

cards.term: Name and year of India’s first programme?
cards.definition: Family planning, started in 1951

cards.term: Current name of the improved programmes?
cards.definition: Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes
Creating awareness about reproduction-related aspects and providing facilities and support for a reproductively healthy society
Government and non-government agencies (audio-visual and print media), parents, relatives, teachers and friends

cards.term: Why is sex education in schools encouraged? (Exercise 3)
cards.definition: Gives the young right information, discourages belief in myths and misconceptions about sex

cards.term: Topics that help adolescents lead a reproductively healthy life?
cards.definition: Reproductive organs, adolescence and its changes, safe hygienic sexual practices, STDs, AIDS

cards.term: What should fertile couples be educated about?
cards.definition: Birth control options, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care, breast feeding, equal opportunities for male and female child

cards.term: What do reproductive health action plans need to succeed?
cards.definition: Strong infrastructure, professional expertise and material support
Pregnancy, delivery, STDs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems, infertility
Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination and massive child immunisation
Some amniotic fluid of the developing foetus is taken to analyse fetal cells and dissolved substances
Test for genetic disorders: Down syndrome, haemophilia, sickle-cell anaemia; determine survivability of the foetus

cards.term: Why is amniocentesis for sex determination banned? (Exercise 8)
cards.definition: To check the menace of female foeticide and a falling sex ratio

cards.term: What is Saheli, and who developed it?
cards.definition: Oral contraceptive for females, developed at CDRI, Lucknow

cards.term: Indicators of improved reproductive health in society? (Exercise 4)
cards.definition: Better awareness, more medically assisted deliveries, better post-natal care → lower MMR and IMR small families better STD detection and cure

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints "aminocentesis" and "haemoplilia" on p. 42. Correct spellings?
cards.definition: Amniocentesis and haemophilia

cards.term: Why did population explode in the last century?
cards.definition: Better health facilities and living conditions

cards.text: World population: about {{c1::2 billion}} in 1900, about {{c2::6 billion}} by 2000, {{c3::7.2 billion}} in 2011.
India’s population: about {{c1::350 million}} at independence, close to {{c2::1 billion}} by 2000, crossed {{c3::1.2 billion}} in May 2011.

cards.definition: About 1.4 billion; India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate)
Rapid decline in death rate, MMR, IMR and increase in people of reproducible age
Maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate
Less than 2%, i.e. 20/1000/year
Absolute scarcity of basic needs: food, shelter, clothing

cards.term: Most important step to check population growth?
cards.definition: Motivate smaller families using contraceptive methods
Hum Do Hamare Do (we two, our two); many young urban couples adopt a one child norm

cards.term: Legal marriageable ages set to check population?
cards.definition: Females 18 years, males 21 years
User-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible, no or least side effects, not interfering with sexual drive or act
Natural/traditional, barrier, IUDs, oral contraceptives, injectables, implants, surgical
Avoid chances of ovum and sperm meeting
Avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the cycle, when ovulation is expected

cards.term: Why are days 10–17 called the fertile period?
cards.definition: Chances of fertilisation are very high because ovulation is expected then
Withdrawal: male withdraws the penis just before ejaculation to avoid insemination
Absence of menstruation during intense lactation after parturition: ovulation does not occur

cards.term: For how long is lactational amenorrhea effective?
cards.definition: Up to a maximum of six months after parturition, only with full breast-feeding

cards.term: Pros and cons of natural methods?
cards.definition: Side effects almost nil (no medicines/devices), but chances of failure are high
Physically prevent ovum and sperm from meeting

cards.term: What are condoms made of, and how do they work?
cards.definition: Thin rubber/latex sheath covering the penis (male) or vagina and cervix (female) so semen does not enter the female tract
Nirodh
Additional benefit: protection from STIs and AIDS
Disposable, can be self-inserted, give privacy to the user
Female condom (Figure 3.1b)

cards.term: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults: how do they work?
cards.definition: Rubber barriers covering the cervix during coitus, blocking sperm entry; reusable

cards.term: What is used with these barriers to increase efficiency?
cards.definition: Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams
Doctors or expert nurses, in the uterus through the vagina
Non-medicated: Lippes loop; Copper-releasing: CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375; Hormone-releasing: Progestasert, LNG-20

advancedHtml.backHtml:
IUDs

Example?

Non-medicatedLippes loop
Copper-releasingCuT, Cu7, Multiload 375
Hormone-releasingProgestasert, LNG-20

cards.definition: Copper T (CuT), a copper-releasing IUD
Increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus

cards.term: How do copper ions in IUDs act?
cards.definition: Suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
Make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms
Females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children; widely accepted in India

cards.term: What are oral contraceptive pills made of?
cards.definition: Small doses of progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations
Daily for 21 days, starting within the first 5 days of the cycle; gap of 7 days (menstruation), then repeat
Inhibit ovulation and implantation; alter cervical mucus to block sperm
Non-steroidal, once-a-week pill, very few side effects, high contraceptive value
Centchroman (ormeloxifene), a selective estrogen receptor modulator

cards.term: Correct: "Oral pills are very popular among rural women." (Exercise 12c)
cards.definition: Pills are popular mainly among urban women; awareness is low in rural areas

cards.term: How are injectables and implants different from pills?
cards.definition: Same hormones and similar action, but much longer effective periods
Under the skin
Progestogens, progestogen–estrogen combinations or IUDs used within 72 hours of coitus
To avoid pregnancy after rape or casual unprotected intercourse

cards.term: What are surgical methods also called, and when advised?
cards.definition: Sterilisation; a terminal method to prevent any more pregnancies

cards.term: How do surgical methods prevent conception?
cards.definition: Block gamete transport
A small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied through a small incision on the scrotum
A small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina
Left: vasectomy (vas deferens tied and cut). Right: tubectomy (fallopian tubes tied and cut).
Highly effective, but reversibility is very poor
They do not stop gamete formation; they block gamete transport

cards.term: Why is removal of gonads not a contraceptive option? (Exercise 7)
cards.definition: Gonads also make hormones; removing them disturbs secondary sexual characters and health, and is irreversible
Nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding, even breast cancer

cards.term: Are contraceptives regular requirements for reproductive health?
cards.definition: No. They act against a natural event (conception); used to prevent, delay or space pregnancy

cards.term: Mnemonic for how each contraceptive works?
cards.definition: Natural = avoid meeting in time Barrier = block physically IUD = kill/slow sperm Pill = stop ovulation Surgery = cut the road
Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term; induced abortion

cards.term: Number of MTPs worldwide per year?
cards.definition: 45–50 million: about 1/5th of all conceived pregnancies
1971, with strict conditions to prevent misuse

cards.term: Why are restrictions on MTP important in India?
cards.definition: To check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticide
Unwanted pregnancy (unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, rape) or when continuing is harmful or fatal to mother/foetus
During the first trimester (up to 12 weeks); second-trimester abortions are much riskier
Illegal MTPs by unqualified quacks; misuse of amniocentesis for sex determination followed by MTP

cards.term: How can these trends be reversed?
cards.definition: Counselling on avoiding unprotected coitus and risks of illegal abortion, plus more health care facilities

cards.term: MTP (Amendment) Act as per NCERT: opinions needed?
cards.definition: Up to 12 weeks: one registered medical practitioner. 12–24 weeks: two practitioners.

cards.term: Grounds for MTP under the Act?
cards.definition: Risk to the life or grave physical/mental injury of the woman; or substantial risk of the child being seriously handicapped

cards.term: Update: NCERT calls it the MTP (Amendment) Act 2017. Current law?
cards.definition: The MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021: one doctor up to 20 weeks, two doctors 20–24 weeks for special categories; no limit for substantial foetal abnormalities (medical board)
True: spontaneous abortion = miscarriage

cards.term: Other names for sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
cards.definition: Venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI)
Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, HIV/AIDS
HIV infection (leading to AIDS)

cards.term: STIs also transmitted by needles, blood and mother to foetus?
cards.definition: Hepatitis-B and HIV

cards.term: Which STIs are not completely curable?
cards.definition: Hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV; others are curable if detected early
Not all. Hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV are not completely curable.
Itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings in the genital region

cards.term: Why do STIs often go untreated?
cards.definition: Infected females may be asymptomatic mild early symptoms social stigma
PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, cancer of the reproductive tract

cards.term: Age group with highest STI incidence?
cards.definition: 15–24 years
Avoid sex with unknown/multiple partners always use condoms see a qualified doctor early if in doubt

Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacterium); Syphilis: Treponema pallidum (bacterium); Genital herpes: Herpes simplex virus; Genital warts: Human papilloma virus; Trichomoniasis: Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan); Chlamydiasis: Chlamydia trachomatis (bacterium)

cards.definition: Inability to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual co-habitation (NCERT summary: after 2 years)
WHO: failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (exam answer per NCERT: 2 years)
Physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or psychological

cards.term: Is infertility always due to the female? (Exercise 11b)
cards.definition: False. More often than not the problem lies in the male partner.
Assisted reproductive technologies: special techniques helping infertile couples have children
In vitro fertilisation (outside the body, in simulated conditions) followed by embryo transfer; the "test tube baby" programme

cards.term: ZIFT: what is transferred and where?
cards.definition: Zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) into the fallopian tube

cards.term: IUT: what is transferred and where?
cards.definition: Embryo with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus

cards.term: Correct: "In ET, embryos are always transferred into the uterus." (Exercise 12d)
cards.definition: Not always. Up to 8 blastomeres → fallopian tube (ZIFT); more → uterus (IUT).

cards.term: Can embryos formed by in-vivo fertilisation be transferred?
cards.definition: Yes, to assist females who cannot conceive
Gamete intra fallopian transfer: a donor ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can support fertilisation
Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection: a sperm is directly injected into the ovum in the lab
Male cannot inseminate, or very low sperm count
Intra-uterine insemination: semen from husband or donor introduced into the uterus
ZIFT = Zygote → tube. GIFT = Gamete (ovum) → tube. IUT = older embryo → uterus. IUI = semen → uterus.
Need high precision, specialised professionals and expensive instruments; also emotional, religious, social deterrents

cards.term: Best alternative for couples seeking parenthood (NCERT)?
cards.definition: Legal adoption of orphaned and destitute children
Periodic abstinence: Natural; Diaphragm, cervical cap: Barrier (female); Multiload 375: Copper IUD; LNG-20: Hormone IUD; Saheli: Oral pill (non-steroidal); Vasectomy: Surgical (male)
